questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a **mathematical proof**?
options: A sequence of logical deductions from given assumptions that establishes the truth of a statement
A numerical example that demonstrates a pattern
A diagram showing a geometric relationship
A hypothesis that has been tested many times
questions.solution: A mathematical proof is a rigorous logical argument that establishes the truth of a statement from axioms and previously proven results.

steps.explain: Identify what distinguishes a proof from other mathematical reasoning.
steps.work: A proof must logically deduce the conclusion from accepted assumptions using valid inference rules.

steps.explain: Eliminate the other options.
steps.work: Numerical examples (option B) are not proofs — they may show a pattern but cannot establish universal truth. Diagrams (option C) can illustrate but not prove. A hypothesis (option D) is unproven conjecture.

steps.explain: State the correct definition.
steps.work: Option A correctly defines a proof as a sequence of logical deductions from given assumptions.

questions.stem: In a proof by **direct method**, we:
options: Assume the conclusion is false and derive a contradiction
Assume the negation of the hypothesis and prove the negation of the conclusion
Start from the hypothesis and use logical steps to reach the conclusion
Test specific numerical examples to confirm the result
questions.solution: In a direct proof, we start from the hypothesis (given conditions) and use logical steps to arrive at the conclusion.

steps.explain: Recall the definition of a direct proof.
steps.work: A direct proof starts with the hypothesis \(P\) and uses axioms, definitions, and previously established results to prove the conclusion \(Q\), establishing \(P \Rightarrow Q\).

steps.explain: Distinguish from other proof types.
steps.work: Option A is proof by contradiction. Option B is proof by contrapositive. Option D is not a proof method at all.

questions.hint: A counter-example to 'if P then Q' is a case where P is true and Q is false.

questions.stem:
Consider the statement for \(n\in\mathbb{N}\):

If \(n\) is prime then \(n\) has exactly two factors.

parts.hint: Converse of P ⇒ Q is Q ⇒ P.

steps.explain: Label the parts of the statement \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
steps.work: \(P:\ n\text{ is prime},\qquad Q:\ n\text{ has exactly two factors}\)

steps.explain: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion: \(Q\Rightarrow P\).

So the converse is: if \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime. (Option 'if not prime then not two factors' is the inverse \(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\); 'if not two factors then not prime' is the contrapositive.)

options: If \(n\) is not prime then \(n\) does not have exactly two factors.
If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime.
If \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime.
If \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime.

keyPoints.note: The converse swaps the 'if' part and the 'then' part.

parts.hint: Contrapositive of P ⇒ Q is (not Q) ⇒ (not P).

steps.explain: With \(P:\ n\) is prime and \(Q:\ n\) has exactly two factors, the contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\): swap and negate both parts.
So: if \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime. A statement and its contrapositive are always logically equivalent.

options: If \(n\) is not prime then \(n\) does not have exactly two factors.
If \(n\) is prime then \(n\) does not have exactly two factors.
If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is not prime.
If \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime.

keyPoints.note: Swap the two parts AND negate both.

parts.stem: Determine whether or not the statement is an equivalence. Give reasons.
parts.hint: An equivalence needs the statement AND its converse to be true.

steps.explain: \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\) (an equivalence) means both \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and its converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\) are true.
\(P\Rightarrow Q\) is true: a prime has exactly the two factors 1 and itself.

\(Q\Rightarrow P\) is also true: if \(n\) has exactly two factors, they must be 1 and \(n\) (with \(n\neq1\)), which is the definition of a prime. (1 has only one factor, so it is not a counter-example.)
Both directions hold, so the statement is an equivalence. Note the contrapositive is always equivalent to the statement, so it cannot be used as the reason.

options: It is an equivalence, because the statement and its contrapositive are both true.
It is an equivalence: the statement is true and its converse (if \(n\) has exactly two factors then \(n\) is prime) is also true.
It is not an equivalence, because the converse is false for \(n=1\).
It is not an equivalence, because a statement and its contrapositive are never both true.

keyPoints.text: whether or not the statement is an equivalence
keyPoints.note: Check whether the converse (from (i)) is also true.

parts.stem:
Georg said that:

If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is composite.

Determine whether or not this statement is true. If not, give a counter-example.
parts.hint: Natural numbers are prime, composite, or … one more case.

steps.explain: A composite number has more than two factors. So the statement says: if \(n\) does not have exactly two factors, it has more than two.
Look for an \(n\) without exactly two factors that is not composite. \(n=1\) has exactly one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.
So the statement is false, with counter-example \(n=1\). (\(n=4\) is composite, so it agrees with the statement; \(n=2\) does not satisfy the hypothesis.)

options: It is true, because every number that is not prime is composite.
It is false. Counter-example: \(n=4\) does not have exactly two factors.
It is false. Counter-example: \(n=2\) has exactly two factors.
It is false. Counter-example: \(n=1\) has only one factor but is not composite.

keyPoints.text: If \(n\) does not have exactly two factors then \(n\) is composite
keyPoints.note: Think about n = 1: how many factors does it have, and is it composite?

questions.stem:
Write the negation of the statement:

All meerkats eat grubs.
questions.hint: The negation of 'all … do' is 'at least one … does not'.

steps.explain: The statement is 'for all meerkats, it eats grubs'.
The negation of 'for all' is 'there exists one that does not'.
So the negation is: at least one meerkat does not eat grubs. 'No meerkats eat grubs' is too strong — it is not the negation.

options: All animals that eat grubs are meerkats.
At least one meerkat does not eat grubs.

keyPoints.note: Negating 'all' gives 'there exists at least one that does not'.

questions.stem:
Consider the following proposition.
“If a positive integer is not a perfect square, then it is not prime.”
If a number was found which had the following properties, which would be a counterexample to the proposition?
questions.hint: A counterexample to 'if P then Q' has P true and Q false.

steps.explain: The proposition has the form \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
A counterexample makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false: \(P\) true and \(Q\) false.
\(Q\) false means the number IS prime. So we need a number that is not a perfect square and is prime (e.g. 7): option A.

options: A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is not a perfect square and is not prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is prime.
A positive integer that is a perfect square and is not prime.

keyPoints.note: Make the 'if' part true and the 'then' part false.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is the contrapositive of the statement
“if \(x\gt y\gt 0\) then \(0\lt\frac{1}{x}\lt\frac{1}{y}\)” ?
questions.hint: Contrapositive: not Q ⇒ not P. A squeezed inequality is an 'and', so its negation is an 'or'.

steps.explain: The contrapositive of \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\).
A chain like \(0\lt\frac1x\lt\frac1y\) means two conditions joined by 'and': \(0\lt\frac1x\) together with \(\frac1x\lt\frac1y\). Negating an 'and' gives an 'or' of the negations.
Similarly \(\neg P\) is: \(x\le y\) or \(y\le 0\).
So the contrapositive is option A. Options C and D keep a squeezed chain, which wrongly stays an 'and'.

keyPoints.note: Negate both parts and swap them. 'a < b < c' means a < b AND b < c, whose negation is an OR.

questions.stem:
The following slogan is used at a particular swimming centre.
“If you are a strong swimmer, then you are unlikely to drown.”
Which of the following statements is logically equivalent to the above slogan?
questions.hint: Logically equivalent = contrapositive.

steps.explain: Label the slogan \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
Only the contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) is always logically equivalent to \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
\(\neg Q\): likely to drown. \(\neg P\): not a strong swimmer. So: if you are likely to drown, then you are not a strong swimmer — D.
A is the converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\), C is the inverse \(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\); neither is equivalent. B contradicts the slogan.

options: If you are unlikely to drown, then you are a strong swimmer.
If you are a strong swimmer, then you are likely to drown.
If you are not a strong swimmer, then you are likely to drown.
If you are likely to drown, then you are not a strong swimmer.

keyPoints.note: Swap and negate both parts of the slogan.

questions.stem: Which of the following statement is true?
questions.hint: Test each statement with a counterexample; watch the order of ∀ and ∃.

steps.explain: A says every real \(x\) has a \(y\) with \(xy=10\). Test \(x=0\): \(0\cdot y=0\neq10\) for every \(y\). So A is false (one counterexample is enough).
B says every real \(x\) has a real \(y\) equal to \(x^2\). That is always possible: just choose \(y=x^2\), which is a real number. So B is true.
C says one fixed \(x\) makes \(xy=10\) for EVERY \(y\). Impossible: \(y=0\) gives \(xy=0\).
D says one fixed \(x\) has every real \(y\) equal to \(x^2\) — but \(x^2\) is a single number, so it cannot equal every \(y\). False.
Only B is true. Notice how the ORDER of \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) changes the meaning: in B, \(y\) may depend on \(x\).

\(\forall x\in R,\exists y\in R\) such that \(y=x^2\)
\(\exists x\in R\), such that \(\forall y\in R,xy=10\)
\(\exists x\in R\), such that \(\forall y\in R,y=x^2\)

questions.stem: Which statement correctly proves that \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational?
options: Direct proof: show \(\sqrt{2} = p/q\) for integers \(p, q\)
Proof by contradiction: assume \(\sqrt{2} = p/q\) in lowest terms and derive that both \(p\) and \(q\) are even
Proof by induction: show \(\sqrt{n}\) is irrational for all \(n \geq 2\)
Proof by contrapositive: if \(n\) is not a perfect square then \(\sqrt{n}\) is rational
questions.solution: The classic proof is by contradiction: assume \(\sqrt{2} = p/q\) in lowest terms, then \(2q^2 = p^2\), so \(p\) is even. Write \(p = 2k\), then \(q^2 = 2k^2\), so \(q\) is also even — contradicting \(p/q\) being in lowest terms.

steps.explain: Assume for contradiction that \(\sqrt{2}\) is rational.
steps.work: Suppose \(\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}\) where \(p, q \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(q \neq 0\), and \(\gcd(p,q) = 1\) (in lowest terms).

steps.explain: Square both sides and rearrange.
steps.work: \(2 = \dfrac{p^2}{q^2} \Rightarrow p^2 = 2q^2\). So \(p^2\) is even, which means \(p\) is even. Write \(p = 2k\).

steps.explain: Show \(q\) is also even — contradiction.
steps.work: \((2k)^2 = 2q^2 \Rightarrow 4k^2 = 2q^2 \Rightarrow q^2 = 2k^2\). So \(q\) is even. But then \(\gcd(p,q) \geq 2\), contradicting our assumption. Therefore \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational. \(\square\)

questions.stem: Prove if \(x,y\in\mathbb{Z}\), then \(x^2-4y\neq2\).
questions.hint: Assume x² − 4y = 2 and show x must be even; then reach a non-integer.

steps.explain: Use proof by contradiction: assume the opposite of what is to be proved.
Rearrange to see that \(x^2\) is even.
steps.work: \(x^2=4y+2=2(2y+1)\ \Rightarrow\ x^2\text{ is even}\ \Rightarrow\ x\text{ is even}\)

steps.explain: (If \(x\) were odd, \(x^2\) would be odd.) So write \(x=2c\) for some integer \(c\) and substitute.
\(c\) and \(y\) are integers, so \(c^2-y\) is an integer and cannot equal \(\frac12\). This contradiction shows the assumption is false.

questions.answer: Proof by contradiction. Suppose there are integers \(x,y\) with \(x^2-4y=2\). Then \(x^2=4y+2=2(2y+1)\) is even, so \(x\) is even; write \(x=2c\) with \(c\in\mathbb Z\). Then \(4c^2-4y=2\), so \(c^2-y=\frac12\). But \(c^2-y\) is an integer, which is a contradiction. Hence \(x^2-4y\neq2\) for all integers \(x,y\).

keyPoints.note: Assume x² − 4y = 2. Then x² is even, so x = 2c, which leads to c² − y = ½.

Prove the following statement for positive \(n\) using a proof by contradiction.
“For each irrational number \(n\), \(\sqrt{n}\) is also irrational.”

steps.explain: Assume the opposite: \(n\) is irrational but \(\sqrt n\) is rational.

\(a^2\) and \(b^2\) are integers (and \(b^2\neq0\)), so \(n\) is rational. This contradicts \(n\) being irrational.
Therefore the assumption is false: \(\sqrt n\) is irrational.

questions.answer: Suppose n > 0 is irrational but \(\sqrt n\) is rational, say \(\sqrt n=\frac ab\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb Z^+\). Squaring gives \(n=\frac{a^2}{b^2}\), a ratio of integers, so n is rational — contradicting that n is irrational. Hence \(\sqrt n\) is irrational.

\((1-a)(1-b)(1-c)\ge8abc.\)
questions.hint: Replace 1 − a by b + c, etc., expand, then use x² + y² ≥ 2xy three times.

steps.explain: Use \(a+b+c=1\) to rewrite each bracket. (As intended in the question, \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) are positive.)

Apply \(x^2+y^2\ge2xy\) to each bracket (multiplying by the positive numbers \(a,b,c\) keeps the direction of the inequality).

questions.answer: (Here \(a,b,c\) are positive.) Since \(a+b+c=1\): \(1-a=b+c\), \(1-b=a+c\), \(1-c=a+b\). So LHS \(=(b+c)(a+c)(a+b)=a^2b+a^2c+ab^2+b^2c+ac^2+bc^2+2abc=b(a^2+c^2)+c(a^2+b^2)+a(b^2+c^2)+2abc\ge b(2ac)+c(2ab)+a(2bc)+2abc=8abc\).

steps.explain: Start from a true statement. The square-root function is increasing, so for \(k \gt 0\)
Add \(\sqrt k\) to both sides.
Both sides are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the inequality.

parts.answer: For \(k \gt 0\), \(\sqrt k \lt \sqrt{k+1}\). Adding \(\sqrt k\): \(2\sqrt k \lt \sqrt{k+1}+\sqrt k\). Both sides are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the inequality: \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt k} \gt \frac{1}{\sqrt{k+1}+\sqrt k}\), i.e. \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{k+1}+\sqrt k} \lt \frac{1}{\sqrt k}\).

keyPoints.note: Begin with √k < √(k + 1), add √k, then take reciprocals (which reverses the inequality).

parts.hint: Rationalise (i) to get 1/√k > 2(√(k+1) − √k) and sum — it telescopes. For the upper bound start from √(k−1) < √k.

steps.explain: Rationalise the left side of (i).
Lower bound: add these inequalities for \(k=1,2,\dots,80\). The sum telescopes.
Upper bound: the same argument starting from \(\sqrt{k-1} \lt \sqrt k\) (for \(k\ge2\)) gives the inequality the other way.
Add for \(k=2,\dots,80\) (telescoping again), then add the \(k=1\) term separately.
Combine the two bounds.

parts.answer: Rationalising, \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{k+1}+\sqrt k}=2(\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k)\), so by (i) \(\frac1{\sqrt k} \gt 2(\sqrt{k+1}-\sqrt k)\). Summing for \(k=1\) to \(80\) (telescoping): \(\sum\frac1{\sqrt k} \gt 2(\sqrt{81}-\sqrt1)=16\). Similarly, from \(\sqrt{k-1} \lt \sqrt k\) we get \(\frac{2}{\sqrt k+\sqrt{k-1}} \gt \frac1{\sqrt k}\), i.e. \(\frac1{\sqrt k} \lt 2(\sqrt k-\sqrt{k-1})\). Summing for \(k=2\) to \(80\): \(\sum_{k=2}^{80}\frac1{\sqrt k} \lt 2(\sqrt{80}-1)\), so \(\sum_{k=1}^{80}\frac1{\sqrt k} \lt 1+2\sqrt{80}-2=2\sqrt{80}-1\approx16.89 \lt 17\).

keyPoints.note: Rationalising gives 1/√k > 2(√(k+1) − √k); summing from 1 to 80 telescopes to 16.

Equality (maximum area) holds when s − x = s − y = s − z, i.e. x = y = z: equilateral.

As \(x\to\pm\infty\), \(f'(x)\to0\): the curve flattens out, approaching horizontal asymptotes. \(f'\) is even, so \(f\) (through \(O\)) is odd — symmetric about the origin.

parts.answer: Since \(f'(x)\gt0\) everywhere, f is increasing. f passes through O with gradient f'(0) = 1 (steepest point, a point of inflection, since f' has a maximum there). As \(x\to\pm\infty\), \(f'(x)\to0\), so f levels off to horizontal asymptotes above and below. By symmetry of f' (even), f is odd.
